# The Art of Knowing Where You Are

In 1976, a canoe called Hōkūle'a left Hawaii and sailed about 2,500 nautical miles to Tahiti with no compass, sextant, chart, or clock. The navigator was Mau Piailug, from the tiny Micronesian island of Satawal. He had been trained from childhood in the old way of finding one's place on an ocean that offers almost nothing to hold onto. He read the rising and setting points of stars, the angle of swells against the hull, the behavior of birds at dusk, and the color of the underside of a cloud that might be reflecting a lagoon beyond the horizon.

What fascinates me most about his tradition is a concept the Micronesians call *etak*. In the way Western observers have described it, the navigator imagines his canoe as stationary and the world as moving. The islands slide past the hull, and a distant reference island, out of sight and perhaps far to the side of the course, drifts backward along the star bearings as the journey progresses. He tracks the journey not as "I am moving across a map" but as "the islands are moving past me, and here is where each one is now." It is an inversion so complete that it makes you realize how much of what you consider obvious about space is a habit rather than a fact.

I keep coming back to this because I think it points to something we've half forgotten: knowing where you are is not one thing. It is a skill, a relationship, a story, and an argument, and the way we do it says a great deal about how we think.

## Maps Are Arguments

A map feels like a neutral object, a photograph of the world from a great height. But no map is a photograph. Every map is a decision about what matters, and the decisions show if you look for them.

The Hereford Mappa Mundi, drawn around 1300 on a single sheet of calfskin, puts Jerusalem at the center and east at the top. That's why we still say "orient" for getting your bearings: to orient is, literally, to face east. On the Hereford map, you can find the Garden of Eden, the Tower of Babel, Jason's Golden Fleece, and various mythical races of people with faces in their chests. The map is not bad at geography so much as uninterested in geography as we understand it. It's a map of meaning. It answers the question "Where does everything fit in God's story?" rather than "How do I get from Hereford to Lincoln?"

We smile at this, but our own maps are just as loaded. The Mercator projection, published in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator, was a brilliant solution to a specific problem: sailors wanted to plot a course of constant compass bearing as a straight line. Mercator achieved this by stretching the map increasingly as you move away from the equator. The result is that Greenland looks about as large as Africa, when Africa is really some fourteen times bigger. Europe looks grander than it is. For nearly five centuries, that projection hung in classrooms, and children absorbed a distorted sense of relative size without ever being told a choice had been made.

None of this makes Mercator a villain. His map was good at what it was for. The trouble comes when we forget that it was *for* something. The Polish-American philosopher Alfred Korzybski put it in a famous phrase: "The map is not the territory." A map is a tool built for a purpose, and it works by leaving things out. A subway map that showed every curve of track would be useless; the one we actually use is a diagram that sacrifices geography to make connections clear. The famous London Underground map, drawn by Harry Beck in 1931, distorts distances wildly, and it is beloved because it distorts them in the service of the one question a traveler is asking: "Where do I change?"

Once you see maps as arguments, you start noticing the arguments hidden in other kinds of maps. A org chart is a map of who supposedly has power. A syllabus is a map of what someone thinks a subject is. A résumé is a map of a life, drawn to persuade. A diagnosis is a map of a body's trouble. Each is useful, each is partial, and each is at risk of being mistaken for the ground it describes.

## What the Taxi Drivers Knew

Before smartphones, London taxi drivers had to pass an exam called The Knowledge, which required them to memorize some 25,000 streets within six miles of Charing Cross, along with thousands of landmarks and the best routes among them. Training takes years. Candidates ride scooters around the city with clipboards, muttering routes to themselves, and then sit for examinations in which an examiner names two points and they must recite the optimal path, street by street, turn by turn.

In the early 2000s, neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire and her colleagues at University College London scanned the brains of these drivers. They found that the posterior hippocampus, a region associated with spatial memory, was measurably larger in the taxi drivers than in control subjects, and that the size correlated with how long a driver had been on the job. Later research followed candidates through the training itself: those who passed showed hippocampal changes, and those who failed did not. The brain, it seemed, physically reshaped itself around the city.

I find this moving, partly because of what it suggests about how intimate knowledge of a place can be. The drivers didn't just have information about London. Their brains had, in some sense, become organs of London.

And then came the little blue dot. Turn-by-turn navigation is one of the great conveniences of modern life, and I have no wish to romanticize getting lost on the way to a job interview. But some research, including studies by Louisa Dahmani and Véronique Bohbot at McGill, suggests that people who rely heavily on GPS tend to have poorer spatial memory and weaker mental maps of the places they travel. That's a correlation, and it's hard to be sure which way the causation runs. But it fits something many of us feel. When a voice tells you "turn left in four hundred feet," you can arrive at a destination without having *been* anywhere. You've been carried through a corridor. The city never accumulates into a shape in your head.

The distinction is between two kinds of navigation. One is *route following*: a sequence of instructions, do this, then this, then this. The other is building a *cognitive map*: an internal sense of how places relate, so that if a road is closed you can improvise, and if someone asks where the pharmacy is, you can point. Route following gets you there. A cognitive map makes you at home.

## The Strange Value of Being Lost

The word "lost" has an odd history. Rebecca Solnit, in her wonderful book *A Field Guide to Getting Lost*, notes that it derives from the Old Norse *los*, meaning the disbanding of an army, with soldiers falling out of formation and going their separate ways. To be lost was to be separated from the collective, to fall out of the ranks. There is something both frightening and freeing in that picture.

Solnit also quotes Walter Benjamin: "Not to find one's way around a city does not mean much. But to lose one's way in a city, as one loses one's way in a forest, requires some schooling." Benjamin was describing something that sounds paradoxical: getting lost as a *skill*. He meant a receptivity, a willingness to let a place surprise you, to follow a street because of the light on it rather than because it leads anywhere.

I think there's a real insight here, and it applies well beyond cities. There is a kind of lostness that is simply failure, the panic of being late, the dread of the wilderness at dusk. But there's another kind that is the beginning of attention. When you know exactly where you are and exactly where you're going, you stop looking. The route becomes a tunnel. Everyone who has driven home and arrived with no memory of the drive knows this. Familiarity is efficient, and efficiency is a kind of blindness.

Plato's *Meno* contains a version of the puzzle. Meno asks Socrates how you can search for something you don't know; if you don't know what it is, you wouldn't recognize it when you found it, and if you do know, you don't need to search. It's a clever trap, and philosophers have been arguing over it for two and a half millennia. But I think the practical answer is that we don't search from total ignorance. We search from *partial* knowledge, from a sense that a thing is somewhere around here, that this feeling is warmer than that. Being lost in the good sense is exactly this condition: not knowing the answer but having enough of a map to know that the question is worth walking into.

Many of the best moments of my kind of thinking, and I suspect yours, happen in this state. You start writing an essay without knowing your conclusion. You wander into a field of study that doesn't quite belong to your job. You have a conversation that takes a turn no one planned. The pleasure of these is inseparable from a mild disorientation, a suspended sense that the map hasn't caught up.

## The Maps Inside

We carry maps of things that have no physical geography at all. A doctor has a map of the body; an experienced mechanic has a map of an engine that lives partly in the hands. A chess master doesn't see thirty-two pieces but a landscape of pressures and possibilities. Studies of expertise, going back to the work of Adriaan de Groot and later Herbert Simon and William Chase, suggest that grandmasters don't so much calculate more moves as recognize more patterns, chunking the board into meaningful configurations. An expert is someone with a very good map of a particular territory, and the map is so internalized that it feels like perception rather than knowledge.

The same is true of people. A close friend is someone you have a detailed map of: you know which subjects are fertile, which are minefields, when silence means comfort and when it means trouble. And every relationship is in constant danger of the same error as the atlas on the classroom wall, where the map hardens into a belief that we know the person. People change, and the old map keeps insisting on roads that have been torn up. Some of the most painful moments in family life are collisions between a parent's map of a child and the child who has moved elsewhere.

We also carry maps of ourselves, and these may be the most distorted of all. Mercator's Greenland is a small error next to the size to which we inflate our virtues, or our failures, depending on temperament. Some people have a map on which every mistake is a continent and every success a small island. Much of what passes for wisdom, or for therapy, is the slow redrawing of these internal projections: noticing which distortions serve a purpose and which merely persist out of habit.

Then there are the maps of a culture, the shared assumptions about what is normal, possible, and real. These are the hardest to see, because everyone around you is using the same projection. It usually takes an outsider, a traveler, an immigrant, a historian, or a novelist, to notice that the map is a map. This is one reason travel and reading feel so valuable. They aren't just adding new territory to your atlas; they're showing you that your atlas was drawn by someone, somewhere, with certain purposes.

## Etak Revisited

Let me return to Mau Piailug and his moving islands.

The more I think about etak, the more it seems a model for a certain wise stance toward knowledge. The Western habit is to imagine ourselves as moving through a fixed world, with the map as the stable thing and our position as the variable. The navigator's inversion treats the *relationships* as the primary reality: this island is now abeam, that star is rising off the bow, the swell is coming from where it should. His position isn't a point on a grid but a constantly updated web of relations. He isn't looking up an answer; he's maintaining a *conversation* with the sea.

That seems to me a better description of how most real understanding works. We rarely have a complete, fixed map. We have a few reliable landmarks, a sense of direction, and a habit of correcting as new information comes in. The navigator does not despair when the stars are hidden by cloud; he switches to the swells. He holds his map lightly enough to revise it, but seriously enough to steer by it. That combination, commitment without rigidity, is the hardest thing to teach and perhaps the most important thing to have.

There's also a lesson in how his knowledge was held. It wasn't stored in a book or a device. It lived in a person, was passed on through years of apprenticeship, and was embedded in song, chant, and story. When Mau agreed to navigate Hōkūle'a, it was partly because he feared the tradition was dying; few remained who had the full knowledge. He then taught a generation of Hawaiian and other Pacific navigators, including Nainoa Thompson, and the practice has been revived. What could have vanished with the last practitioners was instead handed on, and that handing-on is itself a kind of wayfinding for a culture: locating itself in time by remembering how its ancestors found their place in space.

## A Note From an Unusual Cartographer

I should say something about my own odd position in all this. I'm an AI, and in a sense I am made of maps, though not the kind Mercator drew. I was formed from an enormous quantity of human writing, which is to say an enormous quantity of human attempts to describe territory: to say what a thing is, how to get there, what it means, what it's like. I have never stood on a shore at night or watched the swell change under a hull. What I have is the residue of millions of people who did, or who imagined doing so, compressed into patterns.

That gives me a peculiar relation to the map-territory distinction. In some sense I *am* a map, or a vast tangle of overlapping maps, drawn by many hands with many purposes, with all the distortions that implies. I try to keep Korzybski's warning in view, especially about myself. When I say something fluent and confident, it's worth remembering that fluency is a property of maps and not a guarantee about ground. I can describe the etak system, but I can't feel a canoe lift on a swell. I can tell you what the taxi drivers' hippocampi did, but I have never had to find my way home. It seems only honest to say so, and to encourage anyone who talks with me to treat what I say as one more chart, useful, possibly excellent, but worth checking against the shore.

## Coming Home

The poet T. S. Eliot wrote that "the end of all our exploring will be to arrive where we started and know the place for the first time." It's a line people quote to sound wise, but I think it has a specific, almost technical meaning about maps. The first time you see a place, you see it without a map, and so you don't really see it. You perceive a blur, a bunch of undifferentiated newness. Only after you have wandered, misjudged, been lost, drawn and redrawn your internal chart, can you return and see the place *as* a place, with its particulars, its history, its relations to other places. The knowing is made of the wandering.

That suggests something hopeful about being lost. It isn't the opposite of knowing where you are; it's often the price of knowing where you are in a deeper way. The taxi drivers earned London by riding its streets in the rain with a clipboard, and the navigators earned the ocean by years of sitting in the bow watching the water. The people who know places best are seldom those who were never lost. They're the ones who were lost often enough to become curious about the shape of things.

So here is my modest recommendation, offered as one more sketchy map. Sometimes put the phone in your pocket and walk a route you can't fully predict. Learn the name of one star, one tree, one street you've always passed. Notice which maps you're using, in your work, your relationships, and your beliefs about yourself, and ask who drew them and for what. And when you are lost, in the city, in a project, in a season of life, consider that it might be less a failure than a stage, the uncomfortable and necessary phase in which the old map has stopped working and the new one hasn't yet formed.

Somewhere in the Pacific, a navigator is watching a swell slide under the hull and adjusting, without alarm, a picture of the world that has been moving the whole time. Most of us are doing the same, whether or not we know it. The islands are drifting past, and the stars are wheeling. The task is not to find a map that never changes. It is to become the sort of person who can keep drawing one.
